name: Weimar Republic
info: Germany's first constitutional republic, from 9 November 1918 to 23 March 1933, remembered for hyperinflation, the Golden Twenties and its collapse into Adolf Hitler's dictatorship.

facts.capital: Berlin (the National Assembly met at Weimar in 1919)
facts.founder: Proclaimed by Philipp Scheidemann; Friedrich Ebert led the first government

t: The republic was proclaimed on 9 November 1918 during the German Revolution, and its constitution was adopted by a National Assembly that met in Weimar in 1919.
The hyperinflation of 1923 raised the price of a loaf of bread from 3 Reichsmarks in 1922 to 80 billion in November 1923, until the Rentenmark stabilized the currency.
The Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 gave Hitler's government power to act outside parliamentary control, which is widely held to mark the end of the republic.
dyk: The name "Weimar Republic" was first used by Adolf Hitler in 1929; officially the state kept the name German Reich, and the term only became mainstream in the 1950s.
ev: Philipp Scheidemann proclaims the German Republic in Berlin and the abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II is announced
Women vote for the first time in the election to the National Assembly, which then meets in Weimar
Germany signs the Treaty of Versailles
The Kapp Putsch fails after a general strike and the refusal of the bureaucracy to obey Kapp
French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr, hyperinflation peaks, and Hitler's putsch in Munich fails
Paul von Hindenburg is elected president and the Locarno Treaties settle Germany's western borders
The Nazi Party wins 37.3% of the vote and becomes the largest party in the Reichstag
The Reichstag passes the Enabling Act, ending the republic in effect

sections.foundation:
By late 1918 the German Empire was economically and militarily exhausted. A rebellion of sailors at Wilhelmshaven on 29 October became the Kiel mutiny on 3 November, and workers' and soldiers' councils modelled on the soviets of the Russian Revolution spread across Germany. On 9 November 1918 Philipp Scheidemann of the Majority Social Democrats proclaimed the German Republic at the Reichstag building, the abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II was announced, and Prince Max of Baden handed the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert. The armistice was signed at Compiègne on 11 November.

A Council of the People's Deputies of three MSPD and three USPD members governed until January 1919. Ebert and General Wilhelm Groener made the secret Ebert–Groener pact, by which the army pledged loyalty in return for keeping its command. In January 1919 the Spartacist uprising was crushed by Freikorps units, and Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were killed after their arrests. On 19 January 1919 women voted for the first time in the National Assembly election, in which the MSPD won 37.9%. To avoid the fighting in Berlin the Assembly met at Weimar, from 6 February to 11 August 1919, and adopted the constitution that gave the republic its informal name.
sections.socioeconomy:
The war left Germany's civilians in dire conditions. Between 100,000 and 250,000 died of disease or starvation while the Allied blockade continued until the Treaty of Versailles. Industrial production fell to 57 percent of its 1913 value. Printing money to pay for passive resistance to the occupation of the Ruhr drove the hyperinflation of 1923: savings became worthless, while debtors and large concerns such as those of Hugo Stinnes, the Inflation King, gained. The Rentenmark, introduced on 15 November 1923 at one trillion paper marks, stabilized the currency.

From 1924 to 1929, the Golden Twenties, American loans under the Dawes Plan supported a recovery and real wages grew faster than the cost of living. The republic extended social insurance, introduced the eight-hour day, a 48-hour workweek, unemployment insurance and paid maternity leave in 1927, and built over 2 million new homes between 1924 and 1931. Germany was predominantly Protestant, at 64.1% in 1925, with Catholics at 32.4% and Jews at 0.9%. Berlin was a centre of cabaret, jazz, film and the Bauhaus. When American loans dried up after October 1929, unemployment rose to around six million in 1932.
sections.military:
Under the Treaty of Versailles the new army, the Reichswehr, was limited to 100,000 men and the navy to 15,000, with no air force, submarines, tanks or large warships. The Reichswehr was formally founded on 1 January 1921. Under Colonel General Hans von Seeckt, Chief of Army Command from 1920 to 1926, it was largely removed from the Reichstag's control, and many historians call it a "state within the state". During the Kapp Putsch of March 1920 Seeckt refused to deploy it against the Freikorps, saying "Reichswehr do not fire on Reichswehr", but it then suppressed the Ruhr Red Army of some 50,000 armed workers, in fighting in which an estimated 1,000 insurgents and 200 soldiers died.

The army evaded the treaty. The Black Reichswehr, a secret reserve organized as labour battalions, was set up in 1921 and dissolved in 1923 after its members attempted the Küstrin Putsch. From 1925 the Reichswehr secretly cooperated with the Soviet Red Army, testing aircraft, tanks and poison gas banned by the treaty and training German pilots. After 1926 Kurt von Schleicher sought broad support for rearmament, and under Hindenburg the army leadership helped decide the composition of governments. In 1935 the Reichswehr was absorbed into the Wehrmacht.
sections.governance:
The constitution of 1919 created a federal semi-presidential republic. The Reichstag was elected by universal suffrage of citizens aged 20 and over, women included, using party-list proportional representation, while the appointed Reichsrat represented the states. The president was popularly elected for seven years, appointed and removed the chancellor, commanded the armed forces and, under Article 48, could suspend civil rights and legislate by decree if public order was threatened. The president is often called an Ersatzkaiser, a substitute emperor.

Parliament was fragmented by class and milieu, and coalitions were short-lived; from 1924 to 1929 three chancellors led seven cabinets. Political violence marked the early years: the right-wing Organisation Consul murdered Finance Minister Matthias Erzberger in 1921 and Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau, attacked also because he was a Jew, in 1922. The Law for the Protection of the Republic followed, but an imperial-era judiciary passed lenient sentences on right-wing offenders. From March 1930 President Paul von Hindenburg used Article 48 to back chancellors without a parliamentary majority: Heinrich Brüning, Franz von Papen and Kurt von Schleicher. In July 1932 Papen ousted the elected Social Democratic government of Prussia.
sections.impact:
The republic's foreign policy was shaped by the Treaty of Versailles, under which Germany lost about 13% of its territory and 7 million people, its colonies and Alsace–Lorraine, and accepted the War Guilt Clause. Reparations of 132 billion Reichsmarks were set in 1921; from 1920 to 1931 Germany paid 23 billion marks. Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann sought revision by peaceful means: the Locarno Treaties of 1925 settled the western borders, Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926, the Treaty of Berlin kept relations with the Soviet Union open, and in 1928 he helped mediate the Kellogg–Briand Pact. He received the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize.

The 1920s saw a cultural flourishing in literature, cinema, theatre, music and architecture: the Bauhaus Building by Gropius, the Grosses Schauspielhaus and the Einstein Tower. Its failure became a lesson: the 1949 Basic Law of the Federal Republic of Germany answered its weaknesses with the constructive vote of no confidence, a 5% threshold for the Bundestag and basic rights that cannot be suspended. The black-red-gold flag named in its constitution was readopted by both German states after the Second World War. Foreign Policy calls it the best-known example of a democracy that ceded to fascism.
sections.decline:
The Great Depression from 1929 ended the recovery. Unemployment reached 4 million in 1930, and in the election of September 1930 the Nazi Party took 18.3% of the vote. Brüning's austerity, which cut unemployment insurance and forced prices and wages down by 20%, is now held to have deepened the crisis and the growth of support for Hitler. In the election of 31 July 1932 the Nazis won 37.3% and became the largest party. Hindenburg refused Hitler the chancellorship in August, but after Schleicher's government failed, Papen persuaded him, and on 30 January 1933 he appointed Hitler chancellor of a coalition in which the Nazis held two of ten cabinet seats.

After the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 the Reichstag Fire Decree suspended civil liberties. On 23 March the Enabling Act passed with 68%, only the SPD voting against, the KPD having been banned. Within months all other parties and the trade unions were gone, and on Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934 Hitler took the president's powers. The constitution of 1919 was never formally repealed but became a dead letter. Historians debate the causes of the collapse, grouping them as economic problems, institutional weaknesses and the roles of individuals and parties, among them the DNVP's refusal to accept the republic.

summary: The Weimar Republic was the German democracy founded in the revolution of November 1918. It survived uprisings, putsches, the Treaty of Versailles and the hyperinflation of 1923, and enjoyed a brief recovery and cultural flowering, but the Great Depression and rule by presidential decree opened the way for Hitler, whose Enabling Act ended it in 1933.
references: Detlev Peukert, The Weimar Republic: the Crisis of Classical Modernity (Hill and Wang, 1992)
Eberhard Kolb, The Weimar Republic (Unwin Hyman, 1988)
Eric D. Weitz, Weimar Germany: Promise and Tragedy (Princeton University Press, 2018)
Peter Gay, Weimar Culture: The Outsider as Insider (Harper & Row, 1968)
Hans Mommsen, From Weimar to Auschwitz (Princeton University Press, 1991)

pointDescs.1918: The republic is proclaimed on 9 November amid revolution, and the armistice is signed on 11 November.
pointDescs.1919: The National Assembly meets at Weimar and adopts the constitution; Germany signs the Treaty of Versailles.
pointDescs.1920: The Kapp Putsch fails, the Ruhr uprising is suppressed, and the Weimar Coalition loses 125 seats in the Reichstag election.
pointDescs.1923: French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr, hyperinflation peaks, and the Rentenmark is introduced on 15 November.
pointDescs.1924: The Dawes Plan restructures reparations and brings American loans; the Golden Twenties begin.
pointDescs.1926: Germany joins the League of Nations after the Locarno Treaties of 1925, and Stresemann receives the Nobel Peace Prize.
pointDescs.1928: Real wages reach or exceed their pre-war level, and Stresemann helps mediate the Kellogg–Briand Pact.
pointDescs.1929: Stresemann dies, and the crash of the New York Stock Exchange in October ends the American loans.
pointDescs.1930: Brüning becomes the first chancellor to govern by presidential decree, and the Nazis win 18.3% in September.
pointDescs.1932: Unemployment reaches around six million, Papen ousts the Prussian government, and the Nazis become the largest party.
pointDescs.1933: Hitler becomes chancellor on 30 January, and the Enabling Act of 23 March ends the republic in effect.

The article gives the September 1930 Nazi vote as both 19% and 18.3%; I used 18.3%.
